title: Saved from Oblivion: How a 1986 Malayalam Masterpiece Got a 4K Resurrection and a Cannes World Premiere
excerpt: John Abraham's 'Amma Ariyan' — funded by ordinary Keralites, made by a collective, nearly lost forever — is now India's sole entry at Cannes Classics. The Film Heritage Foundation's restoration is a love letter to a cinema most NRIs have never seen.
body:
In 1986, a bearded, chain-smoking filmmaker named John Abraham — not the Bollywood actor, a different man entirely — gathered a collective of workers, students, and artists in Kerala and made a film called **Amma Ariyan** (Report to Mother). They had no studio backing. The money came from ordinary people: auto-rickshaw drivers, tea-stall owners, factory workers who believed that cinema could be a weapon against injustice. The result was one of the most radical Indian films ever made.

Forty years later, it almost ceased to exist.

## A Film That Refused to Die

**Amma Ariyan** follows a young man's journey through Kerala after learning of his friend's suicide, blending documentary footage with narrative fiction in a structure that defied every convention of Indian cinema. John Abraham shot it with the **Odessa Collective**, a grassroots filmmaking commune he founded, using real people as actors and real locations as sets. The film was never commercially released. It screened at festivals, in union halls, at university campuses — passed from projector to projector like samizdat.

When John Abraham died in 1987 — just a year after completing the film, reportedly from injuries sustained after falling from a building — the original negatives and prints scattered. For decades, **Amma Ariyan** survived only in degraded copies and fading memories.

Enter **Shivendra Singh Dungarpur** and his Mumbai-based **Film Heritage Foundation**. Over the past decade, Dungarpur's organization has become India's most important film preservation institution, restoring classics like **Sholay** and Satyajit Ray's **Aranyer Din Ratri**. For **Amma Ariyan**, the challenge was existential: there was no original negative. The restoration team worked from a single surviving print, painstakingly scanning every frame in 4K and making careful decisions about preserving the film's deliberately rough aesthetic.

"We didn't want to 'fix' the film," Dungarpur has said. "John Abraham's choices were intentional — the grain, the ambient sound, the way scenes bleed into each other. Our job was to preserve his vision, not impose our standards on it."

## India's Sole Entry at Cannes Classics

The restored **Amma Ariyan** premiered at the **78th Cannes Film Festival** this week as part of the Cannes Classics programme — and it's India's only entry in the section. This marks the Film Heritage Foundation's fifth consecutive year presenting a restored Indian film at Cannes, a streak that's quietly positioned India as a serious player in global film preservation.

The timing feels deliberate. In a festival year dominated by AI discourse and streaming platform power plays, **Amma Ariyan** is a reminder that cinema's most transformative work has always come from the margins: unfunded, collective, stubbornly analogue.

## Why NRIs Should Care

For diaspora viewers who grew up on a diet of Bollywood and Hollywood, **Amma Ariyan** is a portal to a parallel universe of Indian filmmaking — one where cinema is political action, not product. John Abraham (who remains largely unknown outside Kerala and cinephile circles) was making the kind of community-funded, socially engaged cinema that the West now celebrates through platforms like Mubi and Criterion.

The irony is sharp: NRI film lovers who subscribe to Criterion Channel or attend TIFF retrospectives may never have encountered one of India's most important filmmakers. The Cannes premiere could change that. Film Heritage Foundation has previously made their restorations available for international streaming and festival touring — expect **Amma Ariyan** to appear on specialty platforms within the year.

## A Legacy Worth Preserving

John Abraham died at 49. His filmography is tiny — just four features and a handful of shorts. But his influence runs through every independent Indian filmmaker who's ever passed a hat at a screening, every collective that's ever pooled resources to tell a story the studios wouldn't touch.

**Amma Ariyan** is not an easy watch. It's dense, political, and deliberately disorienting. But it's also electrifying — a film that treats its audience as citizens, not consumers. That it nearly vanished, and that a group of dedicated preservationists brought it back in 4K, is one of the great rescue stories in Indian cinema.

Cannes agrees. The rest of us should catch up.
